1.title: GitHub Basics
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: Git Hub Basics. It covers the exam area Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Explain what Git Hub adds to a Git repository. Create a repository and choose its starting files. Choose H T T P S or S S H. Pick a token type and a credential helper. Generate an S S H key. Fork a repository and keep it up to date from upstream. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Course
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the course. Part: Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Verified with: Git two point five zero.one for the local parts; the Git Hub documentation (read twenty twenty-six-eleven to sixteen) for the Git Hub parts.

1.title: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only
1.text: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only. Every Git command in this module was run for real in practice repositories. The Git Hub screens, settings and rules come from the official Git Hub documentation and were not run.

1.title: What GitHub adds to a Git repository
1.text: What Git Hub adds to a Git repository. Git stores history. Git Hub hosts Git repositories on a server and adds team features around them. The repository you push to is an ordinary Git remote, and in the lab a local bare repository stands in for it. The Git Hub features come from the Git Hub documentation and were not run, because they need an account.

1.title: What GitHub adds to a Git repository, continued
1.text: What Git Hub adds to a Git repository. The figure shows this: A Git Hub repository drawn around a Git repository: the commits and branches sit in the middle, and pull requests, issues, Actions, releases, protection and security features surround them, with clones and forks connected.

1.title: What GitHub adds to a Git repository, continued
1.text: What Git Hub adds to a Git repository. History. Git alone: Commits, branches, tags. Git Hub adds: The same, kept on a server as the shared remote. Review. Git alone: Nothing built in. Git Hub adds: Pull requests to propose, discuss and merge changes. Automation. Git alone: Nothing shared built in. Git Hub adds: Git Hub Actions workflows. Releases. Git alone: Tags. Git Hub adds: Releases built on tags.

1.title: What GitHub adds to a Git repository, continued
1.text: What Git Hub adds to a Git repository. Protection. Git alone: None. Git Hub adds: Branch protection rules and rulesets. Security. Git alone: None. Git Hub adds: Secret scanning, Depend a bot alerts, push protection. Access. Git alone: Whoever can reach the path. Git Hub adds: Accounts and permissions, for example write access to merge.

1.title: What GitHub adds to a Git repository, continued
1.text: What Git Hub adds to a Git repository. Git Hub names the default branch main in new repositories. You can change it in your settings, and changing it on an existing repository needs admin access. Locally, git init dash b main gives the same name. Tip: Start local repositories with git init dash b main. An older project on master can be renamed with git branch dash m master main before the first push.

1.title: Creating a repository
1.text: Creating a repository. When you create a repository you choose its owner, its name and its visibility: public means everyone can see it, private means only the people you allow. Git Hub also offers to add a readme, a.git ignore template and a license. These community files are ordinary files, so they are versioned and reviewed like code.

1.title: Creating a repository, continued
1.text: Creating a repository. readme. What the project is and how to run it. license. The terms under which others may use it. contributing. How to propose a change. code of conduct. How people are expected to behave. security. How to report a vulnerability privately. .git ignore. Which files Git must not track. Starting from an existing project. Create the Git Hub repository empty. A readme created there is a first commit that your local project lacks, and the two histories are unrelated. Try it. The remote already has a commit, and the local project has its own.

1.title: Creating a repository, continued
1.text: Creating a repository. A plain git pull stops even earlier, with "Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches". The option the allow unrelated histories flag forces a merge, but an empty remote avoids the problem. Tip: Create the Git Hub repository empty when you already have local work. Then the first git push dash u origin main is a plain push.

1.title: Clone URLs and authentication
1.text: Clone U R Ls and authentication. Every repository has two kinds of U R L to push to, and origin is the default remote name. U R L form. H T T P S: H T T P S colon slash slash github dot com slash user slash repo dot git. S S H: git at github dot com user slash repo dot git. How you log in. H T T P S: A token, or a credential helper. S S H: An S S H key. Prompts. H T T P S: Fewer with a helper. S S H: None once the key is set up.

1.title: Clone URLs and authentication, continued
1.text: Clone U R Ls and authentication. git remote set url origin url switches a remote between the two. Try it. Switch the same remote to the S S H form. This does not contact Git Hub. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Clone URLs and authentication, continued
1.text: Clone U R Ls and authentication. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Clone URLs and authentication, continued
1.text: Clone U R Ls and authentication. Password authentication for Git on the command line is gone. Use a personal access token, a credential helper such as Git Credential Manager, or S S H. A credential helper stores your login so Git does not ask every time; Git reads it from the credential dot helper setting. Git Hub recommends fine-grained tokens over classic whenever possible. Unused tokens are removed after one year.

1.title: Clone URLs and authentication, continued
1.text: Clone U R Ls and authentication. Reach. Fine-grained token: One resource owner, selected repositories. Classic token: Every repository you can reach. Permissions. Fine-grained token: Granular. Classic token: The repo scope for command line Git. Public repos you do not belong to. Fine-grained token: Cannot contribute. Classic token: The only type with write access. Limits. Fine-grained token: Up to fifty per user; an organization may need to approve. Classic token: Not recommended when a fine-grained token works. Tip: Never put a token in a remote U R L. The lab showed it stored in plain text in dot git slash config and printed by git remote dash v.

1.title: Clone URLs and authentication, continued
1.text: Clone U R Ls and authentication. S S H keys. A key is a pair: a private file that stays on your machine and a.pub file that you give to Git Hub. ssh keygen dash t e d two five five one nine creates both. S S H keys avoid prompts, can also sign commits, and inactive ones are deleted after one year. To test a key, the usual command is ssh dash T git at github dot com. It needs your account, so it is not run here. Try it. Generate a key in the current folder. For real use, accept the default location and set a passphrase. The empty one ( dash N ) is only for this demo.

2.title: Forks, branches and upstream
2.text: Forks, branches and upstream. A fork is a separate repository, owned by you, with its own branches, issues, pull requests, Actions and settings. Git Hub shows the original, the upstream, under the fork's name. Any public repository can be forked, a private one only if the owner allows, and the fork's visibility follows the upstream.

2.title: Forks, branches and upstream, continued
2.text: Forks, branches and upstream. Lives in. Branch: The same repository. Fork: Your own repository. Needs write access to the original. Branch: Yes. Fork: No. Typical user. Branch: A team member. Fork: An outside contributor. Remotes. Branch: origin only. Fork: origin (your fork) and upstream (the original). Git Hub describes two models: fork and pull, where contributors fork the upstream, and shared repository, where collaborators push topic branches. After cloning your fork, add the original as a second remote called upstream. To update the fork, use Git Hub's website sync option, or use Git: git fetch upstream, then a merge or a ree base.

2.title: Forks, branches and upstream, continued
2.text: Forks, branches and upstream. Try it. Bring Ada's fork up to date. The lab uses a second bare repository as the fork. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

2.title: Forks, branches and upstream, continued
2.text: Forks, branches and upstream. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

2.title: Forks, branches and upstream, continued
2.text: Forks, branches and upstream. A branch such as fix typo pushed to the fork is not in the upstream. When the upstream moves on, ree base that branch onto upstream slash main and push it with the force with lease flag. Tip: Keep main of your fork clean and work on branches. Then git merge the ff only flag upstream slash main always succeeds.

2.title: The GitHub CLI
2.text: The Git Hub C L I. gh is Git Hub's command line tool, separate from Git, and one more way to sign in. The commands below are named here and were not run in this course. Sign in. gh auth login. Create a repository. gh repo create. Clone a repository. gh repo clone owner or repo. Fork a repository. gh repo fork. Open a pull request. gh pr create. Merge a pull request. gh pr merge.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Ada has a local project and creates a Git Hub repository with a readme. Her first git push is rejected, and a pull says "refusing to merge unrelated histories". Why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: The remote has a first commit that her project lacks. The readme is a commit with no relation to her history, so an empty repository would have avoided it.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. git push over H T T P S asks for a password, and her account password is refused. What is the right fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Use a personal access token or a credential helper. Password authentication for Git on the command line was removed, so you use a token, a helper or S S H.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. ssh keygen dash t e d two five five one nine wrote id ed twenty-five thousand five hundred nineteen and id ed twenty-five thousand five hundred nineteen dot pub. Which file does Ada add to her Git Hub account? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: id ed twenty-five thousand five hundred nineteen dot pub, the public key file. The public file is meant to be shared, and the private key never leaves your machine.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Ada cloned her fork, and git remote dash v shows only origin. The original project has new commits. What does she do first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Add the original with git remote add upstream. The new commits are in the original repository, so she needs a remote that points at it before she can fetch.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Cy has no write access to the team's repository but wants to propose a fix. Which model fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Fork the repository and propose the change from it. In the fork and pull model, contributors work in their own fork and propose changes back to the upstream.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A teammate ran git remote add origin H T T P S colon slash slash ada token at github dot com slash ada slash shopfront dot git. What is the problem? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: The token is stored in plain text in dot git slash config. The U R L is saved as written, so anyone who reads the config file or the git remote dash v output sees the token.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does Git Hub name the default branch of a new repository? Answer: main. Question two. Which two U R L types can you use to push to a Git Hub repository? Answer: H T T P S and S S H. Question three. Which token type does Git Hub recommend whenever possible? Answer: Fine-grained personal access tokens.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which command creates an e d two five five one nine S S H key pair? Answer: ssh keygen dash t e d two five five one nine. Question five. What is the usual name of the remote that points at the original repository of a fork? Answer: upstream. Question six. Which two steps update a fork's main from the original with Git? Answer: git fetch upstream, then a merge or ree base of upstream slash main.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Git Hub adds: pull requests, Actions, releases on tags, protection, security features, accounts and permissions. Default branch: main in new repositories; locally git init dash b main. New repository: choose visibility; create it empty when you push an existing project. Community files: readme, license, contributing, code of conduct, security,.git ignore. U R Ls: H T T P S H T T P S colon slash slash github dot com slash user slash repo dot git; S S H git at github dot com user slash repo dot git; git remote set url. Login: no passwords; token, credential helper or S S H; fine-grained tokens preferred. S S H key: ssh keygen dash t e d two five five one nine; share the dot pub only. Fork: separate repository; remotes origin and upstream; git fetch upstream then merge or ree base.
